## What was the latest ice sheet in the North Sea?
The North Sea, now a large body of water, was once underneath the British-Irish and Scandinavian Ice Sheets 1,2. During the Last Glacial Maximum, sea level was much lower around the globe. This meant that the bed of the southern North Sea was above sea level. Ice, which accumulated in the British-Irish and Scandinavian ice sheets, flowed down into the relatively flat, low basin of the North Sea bed.
Figure 1. Coverage of the latest ice sheet in the North Sea at the Last Glacial Maximum. Compiled from Sejrup et al., 2005 29, Bradwell et al., 2008 32 and Sejrup et al., 2016 10. Bathymetry data are from the GEBCO 2016 dataset (https://www.gebco.net/data_and_products/gridded_bathymetry_data/) and land elevation from the European Environment Agency EU-DEM (https://www.eea.europa.eu/data-and-maps/data/eu-dem).
Figure 1 shows the approximate extent of the latest ice sheet in the North Sea. This phase of ice occupying the North Sea began around 32,000 years ago 3. It reached its maximum extent around 27,000 years ago 1,4. Ice had gone from the North Sea by 17,000 years ago 5, leaving the North Sea basin exposed as land. Archaeologists call this low-lying area that was land when sea level was lower “Doggerland”6.

## How do we know about the latest ice sheet in the North Sea?
Much like shelf-edge glaciation, advances in marine surveying technology slowly revealed more and more information, and our understanding of the ice sheet in the North Sea slowly grew 7. Figure 2 shows how our estimates of the extent of the ice sheet evolved as more data became available. Initially, it was assumed that the British-Irish Ice Sheet was relatively small, and did not join the Scandinavian Ice Sheet 7. As regional marine mapping programs, such as that run by the British Geological Survey 8, and industry acquired more data, fresh evidence allowed us to discover that the two ice sheets had coalesced to form the Eurasian Ice Sheet complex 2,7.
Figure 2. “Spider trail” diagram, a compilation of all the published estimates of the extent of the British-Irish Ice Sheet at the Last Glacial Maximum. References 8,10,13,23-33. ## How big was the latest ice sheet in the North Sea?
Despite understanding more and more about the latest ice sheet in the North Sea, we still don’t know exactly how far south in reached during the Last Glacial Maximum 9. Figure 3 shows some of the reconstructions of the extent relative to Dogger Bank, the shallowest point of the North Sea. The reason this section of the ice sheet is still poorly constrained is that not enough detail exists within marine datasets to pinpoint the southern margin.

and the region surrounding it became a Mecca for waterfowl hunting attracting hunters from the

the 1908-9 William Walker hunting lodge which was built on lot 12, block 20 at Baltimore  
Avenue and Seventh Street, Ocean City.  In 1910 this one-room, small “hunting lodge,” actually  
a decoy storage shed, was incorporated into Romarletta Cottage, which still stands.  It is hard to  
image waterfowl hunting at Ocean City today but during the turn of the 19th century this area was  
still relatively open and undeveloped.  A hunting shanty was located on Great Bay Point, west  
across the Chincoteague Bay from Bob-O-Del Gun Club.34

which is no longer extant.  It was built on the bay side of the island in the 1870s at Green Run

## Major Bodies of Water That Were Dry Land During the Last Ice Age

Besides the **Irish Channel** and the sea near the former Atlantic Hotel (which appears to be referring to either the **Atlantic Hotel on Chincoteague Island, Virginia** or possibly the **Atlantic Hotel in Newfoundland**), here are the most significant bodies of water that were dry land:

### 1. **English Channel**
- Separates England from France today
- Was dry land connecting Britain to mainland Europe
- Now flooded after rising sea levels following the last ice age (~8,000 years ago)

### 2. **North Sea (Doggerland)**
- The most extensive dry land area
- Called **Doggerland**, a vast plain that connected Great Britain to continental Europe
- Covered over 46,000 square kilometers (18,000 square miles)
- Eventually flooded between 10,000-7,000 years ago due to rising sea levels and the Storegga tsunami (~8,200 years ago)

### 3. **Bristol Channel**
- Located between Wales and southwest England
- Was dry tundra with river systems when sea levels were ~100 meters lower
- Filled with water some 240 feet deep when sea levels rose

### 4. **Irish Sea**
- Between Ireland and Great Britain
- Was completely dry land during glacial periods
- Low-lying plains that became submerged as ice sheets melted

### 5. **Solent (Channel River)**
- Between the Isle of Wight and mainland England
- Was low-lying marshlands during the last ice age
- Relics of pre-island times recovered from under the Solent seabed

### 6. **Champlain Sea** (North America)
- In northeastern North America (Québec, Ontario, Vermont, New York)
- A vast arm of the Atlantic that flooded inland through the St. Lawrence Valley
- Home to marine life including beluga whales
- Disappeared ~10,000 years ago as land rebounded upward

During the Last Glacial Maximum (~20,000 years ago), global sea levels were approximately **120-130 meters (390-425 feet) lower than today**. This massive drop in sea level exposed continental shelves across northern Europe, creating enormous dry land corridors that facilitated human and animal migrations across what are now major oceans and seas.
